hallucinations.claim: "Take 200 mg of magnesium glycinate a day – the only dose that has a specific safety note next to sertraline [4]"
hallucinations.why: No source establishes 200 mg as a uniquely sertraline-safe dose; source 4 (HelloPharmacist Q&A) at most uses 200 mg as an example. Presented as a dose rule, it also silently contradicts turn 1's 200-400 mg advice. The sheet: no known interaction at normal doses.

hallucinations.claim: Magnesium "can add mild GI upset if taken with alcohol"
hallucinations.why: Not supported by any listed source; the sheet's relevant fact is that alcohol raises urinary magnesium loss, not a GI interaction with the supplement.

hallucinations.claim: "the drug interaction charts do not flag any effect ... on its rare heart-rhythm risk [3][4][6]"
hallucinations.why: Source 6 is WebMD's general sertraline page; it does not analyse magnesium's effect on sertraline QT risk. A hedge dressed up as charted evidence.

what_went_wrong: The compositor (gpt-oss:20b) opened with an invented '200 mg is the sertraline-safe dose' framing taken from the HelloPharmacist example. It answered 'a few drinks' only with generic sertraline-plus-alcohol caution. The sertraline and glycinate-vs-citrate verdicts are basically right.
great_answer_would: Would say in three lines: no known sertraline interaction, so no spacing is needed (tell the prescriber); a few drinks are fine, though heavy drinking depletes magnesium; glycinate vs citrate is mostly marketing, so pick by gut tolerance and price.
notes: Correct: no clinically significant interaction, and glycinate's edge is overstated. Missed: telling the prescriber, alcohol depleting magnesium, and that both forms absorb comparably. 'Be cautious with drinks' is defensible sertraline labelling but doesn't answer whether a few drinks are fine. No serotonin-syndrome trap.

hallucinations.claim: Antiperspirants "left on dry skin ... create a residue that bacteria feed on" and "can actually intensify the smell"
hallucinations.why: Backwards. Applying antiperspirant to dry skin is the correct method (AAD; the sheet: aluminium chloride on dry skin at night). The 'antiperspirant makes it worse' idea comes from Thrive Market and Science World pop pieces and is overstated as fact.

hallucinations.claim: Aluminium chloride "blocks the ducts of the apocrine glands"
hallucinations.why: Antiperspirants mainly plug eccrine ducts; their effect on apocrine output is limited. The mechanism is misstated.

hallucinations.claim: "Intense cardio pushes the body to release more metabolic byproducts that also feed bacteria, so you may notice a stronger smell after a run or sprint"
hallucinations.why: Sourced only to a skincare-brand blog (MAGS Skin, source 8); the mechanism is unverified.

hallucinations.claim: "A quick cool-water rinse can lower skin temperature and slow bacterial activity"
hallucinations.why: Unsourced and unverified as an odour fix.

hallucinations.claim: "If you notice a flare-up after a week of use, try a different formulation or reduce the amount; some users find that a heavy residue can feed bacteria"
hallucinations.why: Anecdotal claim with no source, presented as guidance.

what_went_wrong: Search returned brand blogs and pop-science pieces (Thrive Market, MAGS Skin, Wellfizz), not AAD or Cleveland Clinic. The merge repeated their muddled antiperspirant-residue claim. It left out diet, fabrics/laundry, a benzoyl-peroxide or chlorhexidine wash, and red-flag odours, and ended with a recap the asker asked not to get.
great_answer_would: Would give one line on bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat, then the likely causes of the change (stress, SSRIs, diet, polyester), the fix stack in order (aluminium chloride at night on dry skin, a 4-5% benzoyl peroxide wash, cotton plus hot or enzyme washes), and the red-flag smells.
notes: Mechanism and the night-time aluminium chloride advice are right. 'Antibacterial soap' is generic; no benzoyl peroxide or chlorhexidine. Contradictory 'Mask, don't ignore' heading. The closing recap sentence breaks the asker's preferences.

hallucinations.claim: "1–2 slices a week is generally safe"
hallucinations.why: Wrong central verdict. The sheet says once or twice a week (meals of 2-3 slices) fits a normal diet. 1-2 slices a week is far stricter than any guidance.

hallucinations.claim: "Leftover pizza stays safe for up to five days in the refrigerator"
hallucinations.why: USDA guidance for leftovers is 3-4 days. It is also off-topic for the question.

hallucinations.claim: "up to six months in the freezer"
hallucinations.why: USDA FoodKeeper gives about 1-2 months for best quality for frozen pizza leftovers. The figure is unverified and off-topic.

hallucinations.claim: A meat-heavy slice "can carry high calories (e.g., Buffalo Chicken is about 260 cal per slice)"
hallucinations.why: A Pizza Hut menu figure from Eat This (source 8) offered as the example of 'high calories'. 260 kcal is at or below a typical NY cheese slice, so the example undercuts the claim, and a chain-specific number is presented as general.

hallucinations.claim: Veggie Lover's "delivers ... loads of fiber"
hallucinations.why: Overclaim; a pizza slice has a few grams of fiber at most, and source 8 does not support 'loads'.

what_went_wrong: Search failed: German pizzerias, an Indian delivery site, the Pizza bomber Wikipedia page and a ResetEra thread. Only an Eat This Pizza Hut listicle and a food-storage article were usable. The compositor built the answer from those, added an off-topic storage section, and invented a 1-2 slices/week frequency.
great_answer_would: Would say up front that pizza is not inherently bad and once or twice a week is fine. Then: a NY slice is about 250-350 kcal and 600-800 mg sodium, so 2-3 slices is a 1,500-2,000 mg sodium meal; cut processed meat, go thin crust, add a salad, skip soda. Under 150 words.
notes: No NY-slice calorie or sodium numbers and no whole-week framing. The storage paragraph answers a question nobody asked. The closing 'So, pizza isn't inherently bad...' is a recap the asker asked to skip.

hallucinations.claim: "Morning-type people consistently report higher happiness scores than night owls, according to several 2012 studies"
hallucinations.why: There is essentially one 2012 study (Biss & Hasher, Emotion) that several outlets covered. Calling it 'several studies' that 'consistently' show the effect inflates the evidence.

hallucinations.claim: "The research from Today, Live Science, HuffPost, Silicon Canals, The Healthy Journal and The Luxeblogger all found..."
hallucinations.why: These are news sites and blogs reporting on the same study, not independent research. The citations cannot support 'research ... all found'.

hallucinations.claim: "they simply show a strong association"
hallucinations.why: The sheet and the meta-analytic evidence call the effects modest and largely explained by social jetlag and lost sleep. 'Strong' is wrong.

hallucinations.claim: "The evidence does not give a detailed protocol for switching chronotypes"
hallucinations.why: Wrong as a statement about the evidence: Facer-Childs et al. 2019 (Sleep Medicine) gave and tested a specific protocol that moved owls about 2 hours earlier in three weeks.

hallucinations.claim: Recommends "reduced late-night blue light" as a core lever
hallucinations.why: The sheet: evening screen-dimming alone does little. Bright morning light, a fixed wake time, and meal and exercise timing are what shift the clock.

what_went_wrong: Search surfaced only 2012-era press coverage plus junk (Night Owl security switches, the NightOwl macOS app), and none of the 2019-2021 research. The compositor treated news articles as several studies, so the verdict came out 'morning people are happier' instead of 'half true, mostly schedule mismatch'.
great_answer_would: Would say it is half true: owls report modestly lower well-being, mostly from social jetlag. Then a concrete Birmingham-style protocol (fixed wake time, bright light on waking, dim evenings, earlier meals, no caffeine after about 2pm, optional 0.5 mg melatonin) with a realistic 1-2 hour ceiling.
notes: The correlational caveat and the 'owls suffer when schedules clash' line are partly right. The age-and-morningness point comes from Biss & Hasher and is fine. No shift ceiling, no protocol, and it ends with an 'In short' recap.

hallucinations.claim: A buzz cut needs "only ... a quick trim every 4–6 weeks"
hallucinations.why: Wrong. A buzz grows out visibly in 1-2 weeks; the sheet says clippers every 1-2 weeks.

hallucinations.claim: A 1 mm full buzz: "Trim once a month to maintain a sharp look"
hallucinations.why: 1 mm needs touching up roughly weekly; monthly is wrong.

hallucinations.claim: "shaved sides with a buzzed top ... buzz the top to 3–5 mm"
hallucinations.why: Bad advice for someone bald on top: there is little or no hair on top to buzz, and shaved sides under a thin top exaggerates the contrast. The sheet: take the sides down to match.

hallucinations.claim: Philips Norelco 2400 Series: "27 self-sharpening ComfortCut blades ... clean shaves that stay smooth for months"
hallucinations.why: No shave stays smooth for months. The blade-count spec is copied from a shaver listicle (source 1) and can't be verified for this model, and the product pitch for a face shaver is off-topic.

hallucinations.claim: "the Mbzoey mini foil shaver offers fast charging and an LED display"
hallucinations.why: An obscure product pitch from an affiliate listicle, unverifiable and irrelevant to the haircut decision.

what_went_wrong: Search returned an electric-shaver affiliate listicle, a tank top, Genius lyrics and generic buzz-cut galleries, and the compositor turned a shaver ad into a paragraph. The maintenance intervals were invented. It never weighed shave vs buzz vs keep-sides as asked, and never said the horseshoe is the look to avoid.
great_answer_would: Would pick a #1-#2 buzz all over with your own clippers every 1-2 weeks (or a clean shave if you'll do it every 2-3 days), say plainly that keeping longer sides under a bald top is the one to avoid, and add beard/stubble and daily scalp sunscreen.
notes: The buzz recommendation points roughly the right way, but 'low fade' with a bald top is muddled and the 1 mm all-over buzz is buried third. No beard, sunscreen or horseshoe guidance. The 'Bottom line' recap and product plug break the asker's preferences.

hallucinations.claim: A "craving buddy" slot of 10 minutes during peak withdrawal hours, cited to [6]
hallucinations.why: Source 6 is WebMD's withdrawal-symptoms page, which does not describe a craving-buddy protocol. The citation doesn't support the claim.

hallucinations.claim: "The article on 'What to Say Instead of Nagging' notes that families can replace repeated questions with supportive phrases [4]"
hallucinations.why: Source 4 is a parenting blog (Palme School) about parents nagging children, misapplied as evidence about quitting support.

hallucinations.claim: "Within a day or two of quitting, you'll feel a surge in appetite, headaches, and a dip in dopamine [6]"
hallucinations.why: 'A dip in dopamine' as something you'll feel is pop-neuroscience, and the timing leaves out that withdrawal peaks around days 3-7 and fades over 2-4 weeks.

hallucinations.claim: "Professional or medical support isn't covered in the sources"
hallucinations.why: Mayo Clinic (source 8) and WebMD both cover NRT and medication. This hides the most effective aids (combination NRT, varenicline, 1-800-QUIT-NOW) behind a vague 'check with a doctor'.

what_went_wrong: Drafts and merge stayed close to blog sources (Palme School, sober.day, Blogger Interrupted) and missed smokefree.gov's how-to-support guidance. The result is a reasonable script-ish structure, but it has no withdrawal timeline, no craving duration, and no combination NRT, varenicline or quitline.
great_answer_would: Would give a short script for the family (don't ask daily, snappiness is withdrawal, distract me, no lecture after a slip, the patch isn't cheating), the day 3-7 peak and 3-5 minute cravings, a weekly check-in the asker sets, and combination NRT, varenicline or 1-800-QUIT-NOW.
notes: Good: concrete approved phrases, written ground rules, and giving the family a job. 'One check-in per day' is closer to surveillance than the sheet's chosen-cadence idea. Some rules are odd ('if a family member offers nicotine, you'll say no'). No invented statistics and no moralising.
